beats: Hook (line_qc_thousand_two_qubit_bench): for seventeen years (1998-2015 on her chart, Q25-01 p8) a quantum computer meant a handful of qubits, often two, in one physics lab. Cast for all of QC01 (the six parts cut from her first lecture, Q25-01): the physicist (older, bald with a fluffy fringe, bushy moustache, goggles pushed up, lab coat) and the student (lanky, a tuft of hair, round glasses, striped long-sleeved T-shirt, messenger bag); both invented. No lecturer figure anywhere and never her likeness: her voice and her slides carry her part.
Is a two-qubit machine even a computer? You can only test gates on it, and only its own lab can use it (line_qc_thousand_locked_lab; her clip 12:25-12:55).

Then the boom: in about nine years chips passed a thousand qubits (line_qc_thousand_chip_crowd; tape p8 with the company-logo legend covered, or redraw it as a plain rising band; reuse line_grow for "growing fast"; clip 11:37-12:05 "faster than expected"). Check the counts: a 1,121-qubit research chip in 2023 vs the slide's 1,127.

Anyone can now run programs on real machines over the cloud (line_qc_thousand_cloud_access; clip 13:04-13:29; soften to "real machines": the cloud chips are mostly 100-160 qubits, not the biggest research chip). Leave out the free-access offer she mentions.
Company roadmaps aim at about a million qubits: plans, labelled as plans (reuse line_course_map: a long road still ahead).

The field split into competing technologies, no winner yet: superconducting circuits, silicon spins, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons (line_qc_thousand_tech_fair; companies only in captions, neutrally, never a lab or machine by country).
Does every qubit need deep cold? Strictly only superconducting ones; the others still use vacuum and some cooling to cut noise (line_qc_thousand_cold_vs_room; her answer 17:05-18:58).
Why the field now needs computer scientists: the lab door opens (line_qc_thousand_open_door).
Cover (line_qc_cover_01_01; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the physicist holds up a tiny two-dot chip on tweezers; the student leans on a giant chip covered in pads.
